mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a dental crown to become sensitive after many years?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is not uncommon for sensitivity to develop around a dental crown after several years of comfortable function. Possible reasons include gradual gum recession, wear to the crown material, changes in bite alignment, or the development of decay at the crown margin. While occasional mild sensitivity may not require urgent action, sensitivity that is new, worsening, or persistent should be evaluated by a dentist. A clinical assessment will help identify the underlying cause and guide appropriate management.

mainEntity.name: Can decay develop under a dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Although the crown material itself cannot decay, the natural tooth tissue underneath the crown remains susceptible to dental decay — particularly at the margins where the crown meets the tooth. If bacteria penetrate the seal between the crown and tooth, decay can develop over time. This is one of the reasons why maintaining good oral hygiene around a crown and attending regular dental appointments remains important even after restorative treatment.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my crown needs to be replaced?

acceptedAnswer.text: Signs that a crown may need to be assessed or replaced include persistent sensitivity or pain, visible changes around the gum margin, a crown that feels raised or loose when biting, visible wear or cracking of the crown material, or a dark line visible at the gum edge. A dentist can assess the condition of a crown both clinically and with X-rays. Replacement is not always necessary, but when it is recommended, it is usually to protect the underlying tooth from further problems.

mainEntity.name: Can tooth grinding damage a crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Bruxism — the habit of grinding or clenching teeth — places repeated, excessive force on dental restorations, including crowns. Over time, this can cause the crown material to wear down, alter the bite relationship, or place stress on the underlying tooth structure. If you grind your teeth and have one or more crowns, your dentist may recommend a custom nightguard to protect your restorations during sleep.

mainEntity.name: Will a desensitising toothpaste help with crown sensitivity?

acceptedAnswer.text: Desensitising toothpastes containing potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride may provide some relief from mild, superficial sensitivity — for example, sensitivity related to minor gum recession exposing the root surface near a crown margin. However, they are not a substitute for a dental assessment. If sensitivity is caused by decay beneath the crown, a failing margin, or a tooth-related problem, a toothpaste alone will not address the underlying issue. A dentist is best placed to advise whether a desensitising product is appropriate alongside other management.

mainEntity.name: How long should a dental crown last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of a dental crown varies depending on the material used, the location of the crown in the mouth, the patient's oral hygiene, and individual habits such as tooth grinding. Many crowns function well for ten years or more, and some last considerably longer. However, no restoration is permanent. Regular dental monitoring allows any changes to be identified early, which generally supports better long-term outcomes.
